summary: Describes the VLS protocol from Cabletron, which supports equal-cost multipath routing and recalculates routes quickly when the topology changes. It is a vendor specification published as informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a specification for the routing protocol inside a particular vendor's switch fabric. Every switch keeps an identical map of how the switches are connected, built by flooding short advertisements around the fabric, and each switch works out the best routes from itself to everywhere else. A switch is told the whole path to follow, not just the next hop.

questions: how do switches discover each other
subtitle: Cabletron's link-state protocol for switches: every switch keeps the same map of the fabric and computes whole paths through it.

tldr.problem: Switches that carry calls need to know the topology of the whole fabric and to find a path through it quickly when something changes, without flooding the network with routing traffic.
tldr.mechanism: VLSP gives every switch the same topology database, built by flooding link state advertisements, and each switch then computes its own best-path trees with itself as the root. It runs at the MAC layer rather than over IP, and returns a complete list of ports to traverse rather than a next hop.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and describes a vendor protocol for Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN product rather than an Internet standard. It reports equal-cost multipath routing with up to three paths per destination, and its own security section says security concerns are not addressed.

today: RFC 2642 is an Informational memo from August 1999 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a vendor specification for Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN product rather than an Internet standard, and its own security section says that security concerns are not addressed in the document.

sections.title: What the Protocol Is For
sections.content:
The Virtual LAN Link State Protocol (VLSP) is part of the InterSwitch Message Protocol (ISMP), which provides interswitch communication between switches running Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN product. VLSP is used to determine and maintain a fully connected mesh topology graph of the switch fabric. Each switch maintains an identical database describing the topology, and call-originating switches use that database to determine the path over which to route a call connection.

VLSP provides support for equal-cost multipath routing, and recalculates routes quickly in the face of topological changes, using a minimum of routing protocol traffic.

ISMP provides a consistent method of encapsulating and transmitting control messages between the switches. For topology, each switch maintains a distributed topology of the fabric by exchanging control messages with its neighbours: Interswitch Keepalive messages announce a switch's existence and establish the topology of the fabric; Interswitch Spanning Tree BPDU messages and Interswitch Remote Blocking messages determine and maintain a loop-free flood path used for all undirected interswitch messages; and Interswitch Link State messages, which is the VLS protocol, determine and maintain the mesh topology graph. For address resolution, Interswitch Resolve messages resolve a packet destination address when the source and destination pair does not match a known connection, and Interswitch New User messages provide end-station address mobility between switches. A tag-based flooding method restricts the broadcast of unresolved packets to the ports within the fabric that belong to the same VLAN as the source, and Interswitch Tap messages allow traffic between two end stations to be monitored in one or both directions.

VLSP itself is a dynamic routing protocol. It quickly detects topological changes in the fabric, such as switch interface failures, and calculates new loop-free routes after a short period of convergence that involves a minimum of routing traffic. All switches in the fabric run the same algorithm and maintain identical databases describing the topology. Each switch's local state, including its usable interfaces and reachable neighbours, is distributed throughout the fabric by flooding. From the topological database, each switch constructs a set of best path trees, using itself as the root, that specify routes to all other switches in the fabric.

The memo says it is being distributed to solicit reactions to the proposals it contains, and that while the specification may not be directly relevant to Internet research problems, it may be of interest to researchers and implementers. It also acknowledges that VLSP is derived from the OSPF link-state routing protocol, and that much of the document has been drawn from that specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol keeps every switch in step. Each switch announces its own state, that announcement is flooded to all the others, and so every switch ends up with the same map of the fabric. Each switch then works out its own routes from that map. When a cable is unplugged, the map changes, the routes are recalculated, and traffic keeps flowing over the remaining paths.

sections.title: How VLS Differs from OSPF
sections.content:
The primary differences between the VLS and OSPF protocols stem from the fact that OSPF runs over the IP layer, while VLSP runs at the physical MAC layer. Three consequences follow.

First, VLSP does not support features such as fragmentation that are typically provided by network layer service providers. Second, because MAC address assignments are unrelated to IP addressing, VLSP provides no summarization of the address space, such as classical IP subnet information, and no level 2 routing. It therefore does not support grouping switches into areas: all switches exist in a single area, and since a single domain exists within any switch fabric, there is no need for interdomain reachability. Third, although ISMP uses a single well-known multicast address for all packets, parts of the VLS protocol depend on network layer addresses, in particular the AllSPFSwitches and AllDSwitches multicast addresses that drive the distribution of link state advertisements throughout the fabric. Network layer address information is therefore encapsulated in the protocol packets, and is then unbundled so that packets are processed as if they had been sent or received on that multicast address.

Two further differences are worth naming. At start-up, VLSP assumes all network links are point-to-point and that no more than one neighbouring switch will be discovered on any port, so it does not send its own Hello packets over its network ports and instead relies on the VlanHello protocol for neighbour discovery. If a second neighbour is detected on a link, the link is deemed multi-access and the interface type changes to broadcast, at which point VLSP exchanges its own Hello packets with the switches on the link in order to select a designated switch and a designated backup switch. Earlier versions of VLSP treated all links as broadcast, so if it finds a neighbour running an older version of the protocol software it changes the interface type to broadcast and exchanges Hello packets with that single neighbour.

On configuration, OSPF supports and requires configurable parameters, and even the default OSPF configuration requires that IP address assignments be specified. No configuration information is ever required for the VLS protocol: switches are uniquely identified by their base MAC addresses, and ports are uniquely identified by the base MAC address of the switch and a port number. The current version supports configurable path metrics only, with two consequences. All switches are assigned a switch priority of 1, which forces the selection of the designated switch to be based solely on the base MAC address. And authentication is not supported.

Three OSPF features are also absent. There is no periodic refresh of link state advertisements, which the memo describes as an optimisation that eliminates unnecessary traffic between switches. Routing based on a non-zero type of service is not supported, and external routing information for destinations outside the switch fabric is not used.
sections.plainLanguage: The biggest difference from OSPF is the layer the protocol runs at. OSPF rides on top of IP; VLSP works directly on the hardware addresses of the switch ports. That rules out the parts of OSPF that depend on IP addressing, such as summarising addresses and dividing the network into areas, and it means no configuration is needed: a switch is already identified by its hardware address.

sections.title: The Four Operational Stages
sections.content:
There are essentially four operational stages of the VLS protocol.

  • Discovery process. Neighbouring switches are detected by the VlanHello protocol, which then notifies VLSP of the neighbour. If more than one neighbour switch is detected on a single port, the link is determined to be multi-access, and VLSP then sends its own Hello packets over the link in order to discover the full set of neighbours on the link and to select a designated switch and designated backup switch. That selection is unnecessary on point-to-point links.
  • Synchronizing the databases. Adjacencies are used to simplify and speed up the process of synchronizing the topological database, also known as the link state database, maintained by each switch in the fabric. Each switch is only required to synchronize its database with those neighbours to which it is adjacent, which reduces the amount of routing protocol traffic across the fabric, particularly for multi-access links with multiple switches.
  • Maintaining the databases. Each switch advertises its state, also known as its link state, any time its link state changes. Link state advertisements are distributed throughout the switch fabric using a reliable flooding algorithm that ensures that all switches in the fabric are notified of any link state changes.
  • Calculating the best paths. The link state database consists of the collection of link state advertisements received from each switch. Each switch uses its link state database to calculate a set of best paths, using itself as root, to all other switches in the fabric.

Several terms carry a specific meaning in the protocol. A switch ID is a 10-octet value that uniquely identifies the switch within the fabric, made up of the 6-octet base MAC address of the switch followed by 4 octets of zeroes. An interface is the port over which a switch accesses one of its links, identified by a 10-octet value consisting of the 6-octet base MAC address of the switch followed by the 4-octet local port number. Neighbouring switches are two switches attached to a common link, and an adjacency is a relationship formed between selected neighbouring switches for the purpose of exchanging routing information, so not every pair of neighbours becomes adjacent. A link state advertisement describes the local state of a switch or a link, and the collected advertisements of all switches and links form the protocol's topological database.

Each multi-access network link has a designated switch, which generates the link state advertisement for the link and has other special responsibilities in running the protocol, and a backup designated switch, which maintains adjacencies with the same switches on the link so that failover is optimised. The use of a designated switch permits a reduction in the number of adjacencies required on multi-access links, which in turn reduces the amount of routing protocol traffic and the size of the topological database. Neither is selected for a point-to-point network link.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol runs in four steps. First switches find each other. Second, neighbouring switches that have formed an adjacency swap their maps. Third, whenever anything changes, the change is flooded to everyone so all the maps stay the same. Fourth, each switch works out its own routes from that shared map. A link that several switches share elects one of them to speak for the link, so the others do not each have to exchange maps with all of them.

sections.title: Calculating the Best Paths
sections.content:
Once an adjacency has been formed and the two switches have synchronized their databases, each switch in the adjacency calculates the best path to all other switches in the fabric, using itself as the root of each path. In this context, best path means the path with the lowest total cost metric across all hops. If there are multiple paths with the same, lowest, total cost metric, they are all calculated. Best paths are stored in the area data structure.

Paths are calculated using the well-known Dijkstra algorithm. The memo notes that whenever there is a change in an adjacency relationship, or any change that alters the topology of the switch fabric, the set of best paths must be recalculated.

What differs from a conventional link-state protocol is what the result looks like. Instead of providing the next hop to a destination, VLSP calculates and maintains complete end-to-end path information. On request, a list of individual port identifiers is generated describing a complete path from the source switch to the destination switch. If multiple equal-cost routes exist to a destination switch, up to three paths are calculated and returned.
sections.plainLanguage: Each switch runs the standard shortest-path calculation from its own point of view, and keeps the result for every destination. Where two routes cost the same, it keeps both, up to three of them. What the switch hands to the forwarding engine is the whole route, as an ordered list of ports to send the frame out of, rather than a single next hop.

sections.title: Packet Types and the VLSP Header
sections.content:
Every VLSP packet starts with a common 30-octet header. That header, along with the network layer address information, contains all the data necessary to determine whether the packet should be accepted for further processing. The header starts at offset 36 of the ISMP message body, following the network layer address information.

The header carries an unused octet, a one-octet Type field, a two-octet Packet length field, the 10-octet Source switch ID, a four-octet Area ID, a two-octet Checksum, a two-octet Autype field and eight octets of Authentication data.

Five packet types are defined. Hello selects the designated switch and backup designated switch. Database Description summarizes database contents. Link State Request is used for database download. Link State Update is used for database update. Link State Ack is the flooding acknowledgment. The Database Description and Link State Request packets are used to form adjacencies, and the Link State Update and Link State Acknowledgment packets are used to update the topological database. Each Link State Update packet carries a set of link state advertisements, and a single packet may contain the advertisements of several switches.

There are two kinds of link state advertisement. A switch link advertisement is originated by all switches and describes the collected states of the switch's interfaces. A network link advertisement is originated by the designated switch and contains the list of switches connected to the network link.

The documentation follows the Internet Protocol conventions: numbers are expressed in decimal and data is pictured in big-endian order, with fields described left to right and the most significant octet on the left, and with the leftmost bit of any numeric octet being the most significant bit.
sections.plainLanguage: All the protocol's messages share one fixed header, so a switch can decide whether to act on a message before it has looked inside it. There are five kinds of message: a hello used to pick the switch that will speak for a shared link, two used to exchange maps, and two used to send and acknowledge changes.

sections.title: Architectural Constants and Timers
sections.content:
Several VLS protocol parameters have fixed architectural values.

  • AllSPFSwitches is the multicast switch ID to which Hello packets and certain other protocol packets are addressed, with the value E0-00-00-05-00-00-00-00.
  • AllDSwitches is the multicast switch ID to which Link State Update and Link State Acknowledgment packets are addressed when they are destined for the designated switch or the backup designated switch of a network link, with the value E0-00-00-06-00-00-00-00.
  • LSRefreshTime is the interval at which the set of best paths is recalculated if no other state change has forced a recalculation, set to 1800 seconds, or 30 minutes.
  • MinLSInterval is the minimum time between distinct originations of any particular link state advertisement, set to 5 seconds.
  • MaxAge is the maximum age that a link state advertisement can attain, set to 3600 seconds, or 1 hour. When an advertisement's age reaches MaxAge it is redistributed throughout the switch fabric, and when the originating switch receives an acknowledgement showing the advertisement has been removed from all neighbour retransmission lists, it is removed from the originating switch's database. Advertisements at MaxAge are not used to calculate the set of best paths, and the value must be greater than LSRefreshTime.
  • MaxAgeDiff is the maximum time disparity in ages that can occur for a single link state instance as it is distributed throughout the fabric, set to 900 seconds, or 15 minutes. Most of that time is accounted for by the advertisement sitting on switch output queues, and therefore not aging, during the distribution process.
  • LSInfinity is the link state metric value indicating that the destination is unreachable, defined as a binary value of all ones.

Many interface parameters may be made configurable. The interface output cost is the cost of sending a packet over the interface, expressed in the link state metric and advertised as the link cost for that interface, and it must always be greater than zero. The retransmission interval is the number of seconds between link state advertisement retransmissions for adjacencies established on that interface, and is also used when retransmitting Database Description and Link State Request packets. It must be greater than the expected round-trip delay between any two switches on the attached link, and a typical value for a local area network would be 5 seconds. Parameters that specify properties of the individual interfaces and their attached network links must be consistent across all the switches attached to that link.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the values are fixed by the design, such as the two multicast identifiers the fabric uses and the timers that decide when old advertisements are thrown away and when routes are recomputed even if nothing has changed. Others, such as the cost of a link and how often a lost message is retried, are left for the operator to set, but all the switches on a link have to agree on them.
